chapters.title: The Three Voices Inside You
chapters.sourcePressure: Teaches Parent, Adult, and Child as observable ego states, including Critical/Nurturing Parent, Free/Adapted Child, contamination, exclusion, and unchosen state shifts.
chapters.coreMove: Hear which ego state is speaking before you answer the content of the sentence.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating Parent, Adult, and Child as fixed personality types or a pop inner-child metaphor instead of live behavioral states.

chapters.title: What a Transaction Is and Why They Go Wrong
chapters.sourcePressure: Covers transaction as the unit of exchange and the complementary/crossed distinction, with ulterior named only as a forward pointer.
chapters.coreMove: Map the stimulus and response by ego state so you can see whether the exchange is complementary or crossed.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing communication failure to tone or personality instead of tracing which state was addressed and which one replied.

chapters.title: Ulterior Transactions and the Anatomy of a Game
chapters.sourcePressure: Defines ulterior transactions, then introduces the technical game structure: thesis, antithesis, dynamics, switch, and payoff.
chapters.coreMove: Read the social sentence and the psychological invitation as two different messages before you decide whether to play.
chapters.commonMisread: Calling any bad habit or conflict a game instead of requiring a hidden level and predictable payoff.

chapters.title: Why Games Feel So Hard to Stop
chapters.sourcePressure: Unpacks strokes, time structuring, life positions, and the reason games persist even when they hurt.
chapters.coreMove: Identify the stroke supply and life-position confirmation a game provides before asking someone to give it up.
chapters.commonMisread: Assuming a painful pattern continues because someone likes pain or lacks willpower, rather than because it reliably supplies recognition, structure, avoidance, or position proof.

chapters.title: Life Games
chapters.sourcePressure: Covers Kick Me, NIGYSOB, SWYMD, and Debtor while explicitly avoiding Alcoholic in this chapter and distinguishing game layers from structural harm.
chapters.coreMove: Recognize a long-running life game by its repeated payoff, then refuse the role without confusing the pattern with the whole person.
chapters.commonMisread: Using life-game labels to blame people for real hardship, trauma, poverty, addiction, or repeated external harm.

chapters.title: Marital Games
chapters.sourcePressure: Covers Corner, Courtroom, If It Weren't For You, Look How Hard I've Tried, Sweetheart, and an unnamed intimacy-avoidance withdrawal variant in gender-neutral form.
chapters.coreMove: See how a relationship game protects both partners from direct closeness by making the safer role feel unavoidable.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating marital games as tricks one bad partner plays on an innocent other, instead of paired structures that preserve distance.

chapters.title: Party and Social Games
chapters.sourcePressure: Covers Ain't It Awful, Blemish, and Why Don't You Yes But as short-duration social patterns, while protecting legitimate complaint and critique.
chapters.coreMove: Distinguish ordinary social talk from short games by asking whether the exchange is moving toward contact, action, or only the familiar payoff.
chapters.commonMisread: Calling every complaint, criticism, or advice-seeking moment a game and sliding into cynicism.

chapters.title: Professional and Therapy-Room Games
chapters.sourcePressure: Covers I'm Only Trying to Help You, Wooden Leg, Greenhouse, Stupid, and Psychiatry in helping-profession relationships, with care around disability and accountability.
chapters.coreMove: Look at the helper and the helped together, because the professional role can be the cover that keeps the game respectable.
chapters.commonMisread: Blaming clients, patients, employees, or students while treating the professional helper as outside the game.
mustUseTerms: I'm Only Trying to Help You

chapters.title: Games That Aren't Worth Fighting
chapters.sourcePressure: Covers Berne's good games: Busman's Holiday, Cavalier, Happy to Help, Homely Sage, and They'll Be Glad They Knew Me. Holds that these are still technically games but socially beneficial.
chapters.coreMove: Decide when an ulterior pattern is net positive enough to leave alone and protect the generosity inside it.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating every ulterior motive as contamination and interrupting useful, generous patterns just because they are mixed.
mustUseTerms: They'll Be Glad They Knew Me

chapters.title: What Comes After Games
chapters.sourcePressure: Closes with autonomy as the capacity to live without games, constituted by awareness, spontaneity, and intimacy, while naming their failure modes and rarity.
chapters.coreMove: Use awareness, spontaneity, and intimacy as direction markers without turning them into new practices or performances.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning autonomy into a life-coach technique, a mindfulness routine, or permanent independence from other people.
